  application-level caches (like Java's
  or Chrome's DNS caches) add another
  layer above that.

  Each cached record carries a TTL (time
  to live), set by the authoritative
  zone. The resolver decrements TTLs as
  time passes, and once a record's TTL
  expires it must be re-fetched from the
  authoritative source. TTLs trade
  freshness against load: short TTLs
  (30–300s) propagate changes quickly but
   increase query volume; long TTLs
  (hours to days) reduce traffic but mean
   stale records linger after changes
  like server migrations.

  A subtle but important detail is
  negative caching: RFC 2308 says
  resolvers should also cache NXDOMAIN
  and NODATA responses so that lookups
  for nonexistent names don't hammer
  authoritative servers.

  Caching can cause real-world headaches:
   DNS-based failover is slowed by stale
  caches, CDN steering can serve a user a
   far-off node, and misconfigured
  resolvers that ignore TTLs cause broken
   deployments. Operators mitigate this
  by lowering TTLs before planned
  changes, flushing caches explicitly
  (ipconfig /flushdns, res
